forms.explanation: Conditional of vouloir, the standard polite way to order in the first person. The plain present (je veux, elle veut) states what someone wants; je veux can sound blunt when ordering.
Present of avoir with inverted vous, used to ask politely whether something is available: Avez-vous du lait d'avoine ? Quelles tailles avez-vous ?
Partitive du marks an unspecified amount of a masculine noun. Compare du café noir (some black coffee, Reader line 3) with un café noir (one black coffee, one drink).

internalNotes: GATES: reviewed=false and readyForLearner=false throughout. No qualified French reviewer has approved any string here; this is a private corrected candidate only.

PAIRING: English is not restated or altered here except in the fields the schema requires (verb meanings and examples, mode modelEnglish), which copy the source native strings verbatim. frenchCards[i] pairs by index with source words[i].en (18) and frenchReader[i] with source passage.native[i] (8).
PROVENANCE: worked only from the pasted source, draft, candidate and critique. The source file and its SHA256 (8c00629a...) were not opened or re-verified in this pass.

BLACK COFFEE AMBIGUITY: the source pairs English 'black coffee' with Spanish 'café americano', noting 'Usually espresso with hot water; the name can vary by place.' French 'un café noir' translates the English gloss 'black coffee' only. It is NOT asserted to equal an americano; in French usage café noir is simply coffee without milk and is often an espresso. An americano-style drink is more often called café allongé or café américain, but neither has been confirmed for this lesson. Card 1 and Reader line 3 keep café noir pending a reviewer decision.

SETTING: the source scenario reportedly mentions a Roman setting, but the source lines supplied are setting-neutral. No Rome or Italy reference was added to any French string. The draft's 'In France...' regional note is equally unverified and is not carried into any learner string.

PRONOUN MAPPING: the Spanish paradigm has five slots (yo, tú, él_ella_usted, nosotros, ellos_ustedes). French gets six: usted and ustedes both map to vous, and ellos/ellas map to ils/elles. Source '¿Tiene...?' (usted) therefore becomes 'Avez-vous...?' and '¿Qué tamaños tienen?' (ustedes) becomes '...avez-vous ?'.

VERB FORMS: bare forms are given; je elides before a vowel (j'ai). Spanish stem-change notes (e to ie, e to i) do not apply to French and are removed. French irregularities: vouloir (veux/voulons/veulent), prendre (prends/prenons/prennent), avoir (ai/as/a/avons/avez/ont).

VOULOIR: narrative 'She wants' is the plain present 'Elle veut' (Reader line 4, verb example, write mode). 'Je voudrais' stays only in card 15, the type mode and the speaking model; it is a deliberate polite adaptation of 'Quiero' / 'I want', since literal 'Je veux' is possible but can sound blunt.

DEMANDER / COMMANDER: French demander covers both 'ask (a question)' (preguntar) and 'ask for' (pedir), so Reader line 7 uses demander twice, mirroring 'asks for ... and asks'. commander means 'to order' and is the mapped verb for pedir; its example 'Elle commande le café chaud.' drifts slightly from 'She asks for the coffee hot.' Exact-parity alternative: 'Elle demande le café chaud.'

TOMAR: remapped from boire to prendre, which covers both source glosses ('to take': prendre une table; 'to drink': prendre un café). The source example's second verb, bebe, is rendered boit. boire alone covers only 'to drink'.
CARD 13 / READER 2: changed from 'avez-vous' to 'y a-t-il' to match 'are there' / hay.
CARD 14: changed from 'proposez-vous' to 'avez-vous' to match 'do you have' / tienen; this was not raised in the critique. The hear mode model and the speaking model were aligned to it.

CARD 3: 'moyen' is kept as the bare adjective to match 'medium' / mediano. In context it agrees with taille (feminine): 'de taille moyenne'. A medium size is not universal; the learner should ask which sizes exist.

CARD 17 / READER 7: both now use 'C'est sur place ou à emporter ?'. The source has the traveler, not the barista, asking this in line 7; that is preserved as written, although the source's own note says cafés often ask it of the customer.

CARD 18: 'Je peux l'avoir chaud, s'il vous plaît ?' is an idiomatic adaptation of 'Can it be hot, please?'; the structure differs (literally 'Can I have it hot') and l' has no antecedent on a standalone card.
CARD 9: 'le barista' is the masculine form, as in the Reader; 'la barista' also exists.
READER 6: 'répond que oui' replaces the stilted 'répond oui'.
PARTITIVE: 'de la' from the draft focus is not exemplified anywhere in this lesson; only du is taught (du lait d'avoine, du café noir).
TYPE MODE: fixed-response matching needs normalisation of apostrophes (' vs ’), spaces or non-breaking spaces before ? : », and guillemets, or valid answers will be rejected.
HEAR MODE: requires recorded audio and none exists. Models in say and write modes are reference answers, not the only acceptable wording.
SPEAKING MODEL: rebuilt to cover the full instruction (types, order, sizes, oat milk, hot, on-site). It orders un café au lait rather than the draft's 'un café chaud'.
